title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement:
# Longest Repeating Character Replacement

You are given a string `s` and an integer `k`. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other character at most `k` times.

Return the length of the longest contiguous substring containing identical characters that can be obtained after performing at most `k` replacements.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 100` and `0 <= k <= 50`.

examples.explanation: A single character needs zero replacements, so the longest valid window is length 1.
With 13 replacements out of 8 characters, every character can be unified, so the whole 8-character string is the answer.
With 5 replacements allowed, a 7-character window can be unified while the 9th character stays unreplaceable.

constraints: Function signature: `function characterReplacement(s: string, k: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: A window is valid when you can replace (window length - max letter frequency) characters to unify it.
Shrink from the left when replacements needed exceed k, until the window is valid again.
Track character frequencies in a hash map so max frequency updates with each window shift.

editorial.approach: For each starting index, expand the window while (window length - max letter frequency in the window) <= k. The optimal variant maintains a single grow-shrink sliding window with a frequency map, advancing the left edge only when replacements exceed k.
editorial.why_optimal: The brute force is O(n^2): it restarts a fresh frequency count at every start index. The sliding window is O(n) because each character enters and leaves at most once. On 22 cases the gap was 4.95 ms (brute) vs 1.39 ms (optimal), a ~3.6x speedup.
editorial.pitfalls: maxFreq must be recomputed after shrinking, because removing a character can change the dominant letter. Relying on a stale high count will wrongly shrink valid windows.
